criteria.name: Introduction: mission concept and rationale - Include the following required information: • What is the spacecraft's primary mission? • Why is the mission needed? • How many spacecraft are used and why? • Who are the users (operator and customers)?
criteria.reasoning: Mission purpose (coral reef/ocean monitoring via fluid lensing), need, single-spacecraft rationale and users are all described with references. Users could be more specific about operator vs customer, but overall high standard.

evidence.quote: The spacecraft is intended to image and send data to ground stations for collation and analysis.
governmental and science agencies (e.g. CSIRO, BOM)

criteria.name: Main body: mission design - Present a summary of the mission design using software and/or hand calculations as appropriate - Include relevant screenshots and software files (in the main body of the report and/or appendix) - Include the following information: • Where it will launch from, and using which launch vehicle? Why did you choose this option? • What type of orbit will you use? What are its characteristics and orbital elements? • Will you need to perform any orbital maneuvers? • Which ground control facilities will you use? • How often will your spacecraft be able to communicate with ground control? • How long will the mission last, and what are your plans for EOL?
criteria.reasoning: Covers launch, orbit elements, ground station, duration and EOL with STK screenshots and some hand calculation. However, communication frequency is not explicitly stated, software files are not included, and there are technical inaccuracies (e.g. RAAN interpretation, sunlit-path claim).

criteria.name: Report presentation
criteria.reasoning: Logical structure with headings and executive summary. Writing is generally readable. However, figures lack numbering, tables are unlabelled, reference formatting is poor, and Wikipedia is used as a source.

evidence.quote: This report outlines the intended designs and procedures involved in the construction of a Earth observation satellite
STK 3D view of orbit: 12 hours apart

technical_issues.issue: RAAN 27.33° is said to indicate launch facility location; RAAN in inertial space is not the launch site longitude.
Claims descending path is 'constantly in sunlight'; a sun-synchronous orbit still experiences eclipse periods.
States 'A very high altitude would yield low resolution images which is also desirable' – contradictory and likely a typo.
Vega E is not yet built; relying on it for a 2025 launch is a schedule risk, though acknowledged.
Does not explicitly state how many communication passes occur per day, despite giving an access table.
No STK/PIGI software files are included with the report or appendix.
Figures lack numbers and tables lack captions/numbers, contrary to required labelling.
Wikipedia is used as a source [6], which is not accepted.

overall: A competent but uneven report. It covers the mission concept and most design elements with STK evidence. However, key details are missing (communication frequency, software files, figure/table numbering), technical inaccuracies exist, and Wikipedia is used.

feedback.summary: Your report presents a clear coral-reef/ocean monitoring mission and covers launch, orbit, ground control, duration and EOL with STK evidence. To raise C2–C4, add explicit daily contact passes, include software files, correct orbital inaccuracies, number/caption all figures and tables, replace Wikipedia, and make conclusions quantitative. C1 is strong; clarify operator versus customer.
next_steps: In Ground Control & Communications, state the number of communication passes per day explicitly (derive it from your access table) and include the STK/PIGI software files in an appendix.

In Orbit, correct the RAAN/launch-longitude statement, remove the claim that the descending path is constantly sunlit, and fix the contradictory high-altitude/low-resolution sentence; then re-check all orbital claims against your STK screenshots.

Number every figure and caption every table, replace Wikipedia [6] with an accepted source, and make the Conclusion quantitative by citing your contact duration, orbital elements, mission lifetime and EOL plan.

criteria.C1: You clearly explain the coral-reef/ocean monitoring purpose, need, single-spacecraft rationale and users in the Introduction, with references. To move from 8 to the top of Accomplished, distinguish operator versus customer explicitly and attach a literature reference to each user/need claim.
criteria.C2: You cover launch (Vega E), orbit elements, ground station, duration and EOL with STK screenshots and some hand calculation. For Accomplished, explicitly state daily communication passes from your access table, include STK/PIGI files, correct the RAAN/launch-longitude and sunlit-path claims, fix the high-altitude/low-resolution contradiction, and label all figures/tables.
criteria.C3: Your Conclusion links the design to the mission, but it is largely qualitative. For Accomplished, make conclusions specific and evidence-based: cite your 600 km/97.79° orbit, ~10-minute contact duration, mission lifetime and drag-sail EOL, and address the Vega E schedule risk with a mitigation.
criteria.C4: Your report has a logical structure, headings and an executive summary, and is generally readable. For Accomplished, number figures and caption tables consistently, replace Wikipedia [6] with an accepted source, fix reference formatting (e.g., [1] is a bare URL), and ensure every in-text citation matches the reference list.
